verdicts.quote: “Public applications must use OAuth 2.0… This authorization model is based on Login with Amazon (LWA), which is Amazon’s implementation of OAuth 2.0.”
verdicts.reason: SP-API’s public apps use an OAuth2/LWA consent flow; while requests are also SigV4-signed, per the definition OAuth2 is the primary end-user auth.

verdicts.quote: “Note that in Seller Central, you must have a professional selling account to develop SP-API private seller applications.” … “Public developer s must list their app in the Amazon Selling Partner Appstore.”
verdicts.reason: Credentials are self‑serve, but production/public use requires Amazon approval/listing; only private seller apps require a paid Professional plan. This fits “app_review,” not blanket “paid_plan.”

verdicts.quote: “The following sections show all Selling Partner APIs (SP-APIs) and indicate whether the API is available for seller or vendor accounts.”
verdicts.reason: Docs enumerate many API families (orders, listings, pricing, feeds, reports, FBA, notifications, etc.), indicating broad coverage across the product.

verdicts.quote: “The bundled .mcp.json registers the Amazon Selling Partner Connector (MCP server) at ‘https://sellingpartner-ai.amazon.com/mcp’.”
verdicts.reason: Official Amazon GitHub repo documents an Amazon‑hosted MCP server, confirming an official MCP.

verdicts.quote: “Public applications… must list their applications in the Selling Partner Appstore, which requires Amazon’s approval.”
verdicts.reason: It’s buildable today (self‑serve creds, full docs), but caveats include app approval for public apps, restricted‑role/PII reviews, and rate limits—hence “ready_with_caveats.”
